parts.name: Kerolox Tank S
parts.desc: 12 m³ of kerosene and liquid oxygen.
parts.role: A small tank of kerosene and liquid oxygen: 12 t of propellant.
parts.detail: Kerosene is dense, so this tank holds a lot of propellant for its size. It feeds kerolox engines only; any other engine treats it as dead weight.
pros: Dense fuel: lots of mass in a small tank
parts.real: Falcon 9 first stage: 411 t of liquid oxygen and RP-1 in aluminium-lithium tanks 3.7 m wide; Atlas V booster: 284 t

pros: Dense fuel: lots of mass in a small tank
Good balance of mass and height

parts.detail: Methane is lighter than kerosene for the same volume, so this tank holds less mass but burns cleaner. Methane can be made on Mars from ice and the air, which matters for the trip home.
parts.real: New Glenn first stage (7 m wide) and Starship: methane and liquid oxygen

pros: Best Isp with a hydrolox engine
cons: Little mass per tank, boils off during the cruise

parts.name: Guidance electronics ring
parts.desc: The brain of the launcher: flight computer, gyros, radios.
parts.role: The flight computer, inertial platform and radios that fly the launcher.
parts.detail: A ring of boxes around the top of the stage: the flight computer that runs the guidance program, the inertial measurement unit (gyroscopes and accelerometers) that tells it where the rocket is pointing, the telemetry transmitter, the range-safety receiver and the batteries that run them. With a dedicated guidance section the ship flies more precisely and catches faults the capsule computer would miss: reliability goes up 3 %.
parts.real: Delta II guidance electronics (RIFCA)

parts.name: Miniskirt & support truss
parts.desc: An open truss: light, and a place to hang the pressure bottles.
parts.role: An open lattice that carries thrust loads and holds the helium and nitrogen spheres.
parts.detail: Where a stage does not need a skin, a truss of struts carries the load with much less mass. The spheres, valves and cables bolt to it, out in the open, where technicians can reach them on the pad. On the Delta II second stage the miniskirt and truss carried the tanks, the engine and the guidance ring.
pros: Hard points for spheres and equipment
cons: No aerodynamic skin: must sit under a fairing or interstage
parts.real: Delta II second-stage miniskirt and support truss

parts.name: Interstage
parts.desc: The hollow ring between two stages, hiding the upper nozzle.
parts.role: The skin that joins two stages and shelters the upper engine bell.
parts.detail: A hollow cylinder of skin and stringers. It joins two stacked sections, shelters an engine bell during ascent and gives the cables a protected path. On a real multi-stage rocket it also holds the separation joint; this ship flies as one stage, so here it is simply stiff structure.
parts.real: Delta II / Falcon 9 interstage

parts.name: Centerbody section
parts.desc: The stiff ring between the fuel tank and the oxidizer tank.
parts.role: The structural section between two tanks: where the booster loads come in.
parts.detail: Real stages keep fuel and oxidizer in separate tanks with a short, stiff section between them. The centerbody (intertank) takes the thrust of the strap-on boosters and the bending loads of flight, so neither tank wall has to. Equipment bolts to it without piercing a tank.
pros: Hard points without piercing a tank
parts.real: Delta II centerbody: between the RP-1 tank above and the LOX tank below (Delta II put its kerosene on top, unusually), with the first-stage avionics inside

parts.name: Wiring tunnel
parts.desc: The raceway that carries cables and lines down the outside of the tank.
parts.role: A covered channel for cables and propellant lines along the tank wall.
parts.detail: You cannot run a cable through a tank of liquid oxygen. The wiring tunnel is the long half-round cover on the outside of a tank: inside it run the control cables, the sensor wiring and the pressurisation lines. Protected cables are cables that keep working: reliability +1 %.
parts.real: Saturn V S-IC and Delta II systems tunnels

parts.name: Helium pressurant sphere
parts.desc: High-pressure helium that keeps the tanks full of pressure as they drain.
parts.role: A pressure bottle that pushes gas into the tanks as propellant leaves.
parts.detail: As an engine drinks from a tank, something must take the propellant's place or the tank would collapse and the pump would cavitate. Helium at 300 bar from this sphere does it: it is the lightest gas that cannot burn and does not freeze in liquid oxygen. The composite-overwrapped bottle (a thin liner wound in carbon fibre) is the state of the art, and the thing that failed on the AMOS-6 pad explosion. Reliability +0.6 %.
cons: 300 bar of stored energy next to the tank
parts.real: Delta II second-stage helium spheres; Falcon 9 carries its helium in COPVs inside the LOX tank

parts.name: Nitrogen cold-gas sphere
parts.desc: Cold nitrogen puffs to turn the ship. Simple, weak.
parts.role: A nitrogen bottle feeding small cold-gas thrusters.
parts.detail: The simplest attitude control there is: a bottle of nitrogen and a few valves. No combustion, nothing to ignite, almost nothing to go wrong. The puffs are weak (Isp about 70 s), so it turns the ship slowly and runs out sooner than a proper thruster pack.
cons: Slow to turn a heavy ship
parts.real: Delta II second-stage nitrogen sphere, Falcon 9 cold-gas RCS

parts.name: MLI insulation blanket
parts.desc: Twenty layers of gold foil: keeps the cold in and the Sun out.
parts.role: Multilayer insulation: the gold foil on every spacecraft.
parts.detail: Multilayer insulation is 10 to 20 sheets of aluminised plastic with nothing between them. In vacuum, heat can only cross by radiation, and every shiny layer bounces most of it back. It keeps cryogenic propellant cold and electronics warm. Reliability +0.3 %.
pros: Keeps propellant cold and electronics warm
cons: Useless in air: only works in vacuum
parts.real: Kapton/Mylar MLI blankets

parts.name: Solar panel
parts.desc: 2 kW at Earth, about 43 % of that at Mars.
parts.role: Two kilowatts at Earth, less than half that at Mars.
parts.detail: Solar panels power the scanners, the radios and the life support. Mars is farther from the Sun, so the same panel makes only about 43 % of the power it makes at Earth.
parts.real: Dawn 2 × 8.3 m arrays (scaled)

parts.name: Solar wing, large
parts.desc: 5 kW at Earth. A deployable wing, folded for launch.
parts.role: A deployable wing: five kilowatts at Earth.
parts.detail: A folded wing of triple-junction cells that unfurls in orbit. Five kilowatts at Earth, about two at Mars: enough to run everything and charge the batteries for the night.
parts.real: ISS / Juno-class wing

parts.name: Battery
parts.desc: Stores power for the night.
parts.role: Stores power for the night.
parts.detail: A battery pack that carries the ship through the night and through burns when the panels point away from the Sun.
parts.real: Li-ion ORU, 150 Wh/kg

parts.name: Radioisotope generator (RTG)
parts.desc: 110 W from decaying plutonium: day, night, dust storm, anywhere.
parts.role: A nuclear battery: a small, steady trickle of power that never depends on the Sun.
parts.detail: A few kilograms of plutonium-238 glow red-hot for decades; thermocouples turn the heat into about 110 W (the MMRTG on Curiosity and Perseverance, losing a few percent a year). No Sun needed, so it works through the night, through dust storms, and at the same strength at Mars as at Earth. Very expensive and politically hard to launch.
pros: Same power at Mars, at night, in dust
Most reliable part in the hangar
parts.real: MMRTG (Curiosity, Perseverance): 110 W electric, 45 kg

parts.name: Fuel cell
parts.desc: 2.5 kW from hydrogen and oxygen, and drinking water as a by-product.
parts.role: Burns hydrogen and oxygen quietly into electricity and drinking water.
parts.detail: Apollo and the Shuttle ran on fuel cells: hydrogen and oxygen combine across a membrane to make electricity, heat and pure water the crew drinks. Strong power without panels, but the reactants run out in weeks, not months.
parts.real: Shuttle PRSD fuel cells, 7 kW each

parts.name: Armor plating
parts.desc: A stuffed Whipple panel: an aluminium bumper, then Nextel and Kevlar blankets, then the wall. It stops much bigger debris.
parts.role: Absorbs one small debris hit.
parts.detail: A stuffed Whipple panel like those on the ISS modules: an aluminium bumper, then blankets of Nextel ceramic cloth and Kevlar, then the wall. It stops pieces several times bigger than a plain bumper does, and per kilogram it protects better.
parts.real: ISS stuffed Whipple panels (aluminium, Nextel, Kevlar)

parts.name: Whipple shield
parts.desc: A thin aluminium bumper a few centimetres out from the wall: it shatters small debris before it reaches the wall.
parts.role: A thin outer bumper that turns a debris strike into harmless spray.
parts.detail: Fred Whipple's 1947 idea: put a thin aluminium sheet a hand's width in front of the wall. A small, fast particle hits the sheet and breaks into a spreading cloud that the wall can take. Light and cheap, but a bigger piece still gets through.
parts.real: Aluminium Whipple bumper (Apollo era; ISS Russian segment)

parts.name: Spectrometer
parts.desc: Reads what a rock is made of.
parts.role: Reads what a rock is made of.
parts.detail: Fires a laser at a rock and reads the colours of the spark: every element has its own signature. This is how Perseverance tells basalt from clay from hematite.
parts.real: SuperCam LIBS / Hubble COS

parts.name: Ground radar
parts.desc: Finds buried ice for the return fuel.
parts.role: Finds buried ice for the return fuel.
parts.detail: A ground-penetrating radar that sees metres into the soil. Buried ice is water, and water plus the Martian air is methane and oxygen: the return trip.
pros: Finds buried ice for return fuel
parts.real: RIMFAX (Perseverance)

parts.name: Core drill
parts.desc: Sealed sample tubes, like Perseverance.
parts.role: Sealed sample tubes, like Perseverance.
parts.detail: A core drill that cuts a finger-sized sample and seals it in a tube. Sealed samples are the only ones that count when you get home.
parts.real: Perseverance coring drill

parts.name: Science camera
parts.desc: Stereo and infrared cameras: the geologist's eyes.
parts.role: Stereo and infrared cameras for mapping the site and choosing rocks.
parts.detail: A pair of colour cameras for stereo distance and an infrared camera that sees minerals by their heat signature. The maps the crew makes on the surface start here.
parts.real: Mastcam-Z / Hubble WFPC

parts.name: Weather station
parts.desc: Wind, pressure, dust and temperature, every minute.
parts.role: Measures wind, pressure, dust and temperature on the surface.
parts.detail: Booms with wind, temperature, pressure, humidity and dust sensors. Dust storms are what kill solar-powered missions; knowing one is coming is worth the twenty kilograms.
parts.real: MEDA (Perseverance)

parts.name: Seismometer
parts.desc: Listens to marsquakes to see inside the planet.
parts.role: Listens to marsquakes: the only way to see the inside of the planet.
parts.detail: Set on the ground under a wind shield, it feels quakes smaller than a footstep. From the echoes, scientists measured the size of the Martian core for the first time.
pros: Sees the inside of the planet
cons: Must be placed by hand, away from the ship
parts.real: SEIS (InSight)

parts.name: Sample containers
parts.desc: Sealed tubes for three samples. Every kilogram costs return Δv.
parts.role: Sealed tubes for three samples.
parts.detail: Storage for three sealed samples in the ship. Every kilogram you bring back is a kilogram the return burn has to lift.
parts.real: Perseverance sample tubes

parts.name: Sample vault
parts.desc: A sealed vault for six samples.
parts.role: A sealed, temperature-controlled vault for six samples.
parts.detail: Six tubes in a vault that keeps them cold and sealed all the way home, so the chemistry inside is what it was on Mars.
parts.real: Mars Sample Return orbiting sample container

parts.name: Cheap seals (−$100k)
parts.desc: Saves money. Not rated below 5 °C.
parts.role: Saves $100k. Not rated below 5 °C.
parts.detail: Cheaper seals for the tank joints. They work fine on a warm pad. In the cold they stiffen and leak hot gas: the Challenger booster seal did exactly this at 2 °C, after engineers had warned against the launch.
parts.real: Shuttle SRB field-joint O-rings (1986)

parts.name: Adapter S to M
parts.desc: A conical skirt between two diameters. Added for you.
parts.role: Joins a part of one diameter to a part of another.
parts.detail: Rockets change diameter where a wide stage sits on a narrow one or a narrow capsule on a wide tank. A cone of skin, stringers and ring frames carries the loads across. The design page adds one wherever two sections of different width meet: you never have to place it yourself, but you can choose how it is built.
cons: Mass that does no other work
parts.real: Saturn V S-IVB/S-II interstage (6.6 m to 10 m), Atlas V 5 m boattail, Falcon 9 second-stage-to-fairing adapter

parts.name: Kerolox Tank L, stretched
parts.desc: 63 t of kerosene and liquid oxygen in a tank 2.2 m longer.
parts.role: The large kerolox tank made 40 % longer: 63 t of propellant.
parts.detail: Rocket builders stretch a proven tank rather than design a new one: the domes, valves and tooling stay the same and only the straight barrel gets longer. The domes are the heavy, expensive part, so every extra metre of barrel holds propellant for less mass than a whole new tank would.
pros: Better propellant-to-mass ratio than the standard L tank
cons: Long and heavy: about 67 t when full
parts.real: Saturn V S-IC: the LOX tank alone held 1,266 m³; Delta II stretched its Thor tanks 3.8 m; Falcon 9 Full Thrust lengthened its tanks

parts.name: Kerolox Tank M, stretched
parts.desc: 37.5 t of kerosene and liquid oxygen in a long, narrow tank.
parts.role: A long, narrow kerolox tank: 37.5 t of propellant at the medium diameter.
parts.detail: The classic shape of a medium launcher: a slim tube that fits through tunnels and on railway wagons. The Soyuz core and the Delta II first stage are both about 2.5 to 3 m wide and many times as long. Same domes as the standard M tank, a longer barrel.
pros: Fits medium noses and tails without an adapter
cons: Long: moves the centre of mass as it drains
parts.real: Delta II first stage: 2.44 m wide, 26.1 m long, isogrid aluminium, about 96 t of propellant; Soyuz core stage: 2.95 m, 90 t

parts.name: Hydrolox Tank L, stretched
parts.desc: 27 t of hydrogen and liquid oxygen under orange foam.
parts.role: The longest hydrogen tank: 27 t of propellant for the best Isp there is.
parts.detail: Liquid hydrogen is fourteen times lighter than water, so a hydrogen tank is mostly empty-looking volume. The Shuttle's External Tank put its huge hydrogen tank at the bottom and the small, heavy oxygen tank on top, with an unpressurised intertank between them. Foam on the outside stops the hydrogen boiling away and ice forming on the skin.
pros: Best Isp with a hydrolox engine
Best mass ratio of the framed hydrogen tanks
cons: Bulky and expensive for its mass
Boils off slowly during the cruise
parts.real: Shuttle External Tank hydrogen tank: 8.4 m wide, 29.6 m long, 106 t of LH2 at 2 bar; the whole tank 26.5 t empty (super-lightweight version)

parts.name: Common-dome kerolox tank L
parts.desc: Oxygen over kerosene with one shared dome between them: 67 t.
parts.role: A Falcon 9-style tank pair: liquid oxygen on top, kerosene below, one dome between them.
parts.detail: Instead of two tanks with two domes and a hollow section between them, the oxygen tank sits straight on the kerosene tank and they share a single dome. That saves a dome, a metre of skin and the intertank. The oxygen reaches the engines through a pipe running down the middle of the kerosene tank. Falcon 9 chills both liquids below their normal temperature so more fits in the same tank.
pros: Lightest kerolox tank for its size
cons: One wall between fuel and oxidizer: reliability 99.7 %
parts.real: Falcon 9 first stage: 3.7 m wide, Al-Li 2195 skin, LOX tank over RP-1 tank; 411 t of propellant (287 t LOX, 124 t RP-1) for 22.2 t dry

parts.name: Common-bulkhead hydrolox tank L
parts.desc: Hydrogen over oxygen with one insulated bulkhead: the Saturn S-II way.
parts.role: Hydrogen on top, oxygen below, one insulated bulkhead between them: 26 t of propellant.
parts.detail: Liquid hydrogen is at −253 °C, liquid oxygen at −183 °C: put them on either side of a bare metal wall and the hydrogen freezes the oxygen. The Saturn S-II solved it with a bulkhead of two aluminium skins glued to a honeycomb core, which kept the 70 °C difference apart and saved 3.6 t against two separate tanks. It was the hardest part of the stage to build.
pros: Lightest framed hydrogen tank: 26 t for 3.3 t
Best Isp with a hydrolox engine
cons: A bulkhead leak mixes the propellants: reliability 99.6 %
parts.real: Saturn V S-II: 10 m wide, 24.9 m long, 443 t of LH2 and LOX for 36.2 t empty; the S-IVB and Centaur use the same layout

parts.name: Stainless steel methalox tank L
parts.desc: Starship-style: welded steel rings, methane over oxygen, 56 t.
parts.role: A heavy, cheap, tough tank of welded stainless steel rings: 56 t of methane and oxygen.
parts.detail: SpaceX builds Starship from rings of stainless steel a few millimetres thick, welded one on top of the next, with the methane tank on top of the oxygen tank and one common dome between them. Steel is three times as dense as aluminium, but it gets stronger when it is cryogenic, shrugs off heat that would soften aluminium, costs a fraction as much and can be welded in a tent. The material is fixed: it is the point of this tank.
parts.real: Super Heavy: 9 m wide, 3,400 t of methane and oxygen, rings 3.97 mm thick, methane tank on top of the oxygen tank with one common dome

parts.name: Carbon-composite kerolox tank S
parts.desc: Electron-style black carbon tanks: light and expensive.
parts.role: A small, very light tank wound from carbon fibre: 20 t of kerosene and oxygen.
parts.detail: Rocket Lab's Electron was the first rocket to fly propellant tanks made of carbon composite: layers of carbon fibre and resin laid on a mould and baked, with no metal liner inside, the two tanks sharing one bulkhead. It is far lighter than aluminium. The catch: carbon cracks instead of bending, the cracks can hide inside the layers, and liquid oxygen can react with the resin, so every tank is pressure-tested and scanned.
pros: Lightest tank in the hangar for its size
parts.real: Electron: 1.2 m wide, 18 m tall, linerless carbon-composite LOX and RP-1 tanks with a common bulkhead; up to 40 % lighter than aluminium

parts.name: Steel balloon tank M (kerolox)
parts.desc: Atlas-style: stainless steel as thin as paper, held up by gas pressure.
parts.role: A tank with no frame at all: thin steel kept rigid by the pressure inside, like a balloon.
parts.detail: The Atlas missile had no stringers and no ring frames. Its tank was stainless steel thinner than a coin, welded into a tube and kept rigid by the gas inside, exactly like a balloon. It is the lightest tank ever flown for its size. It is also unforgiving: let the pressure drop and the tank crumples under its own weight. Atlas tanks were kept filled with nitrogen from the factory to the launch.
pros: Extremely light: 57.5 t of propellant for under 2 t
cons: Must stay pressurised every minute: reliability 98.8 %
parts.real: Atlas D: 3.05 m wide, needed 5 psi (34 kPa) of nitrogen even when empty; without its booster engines the empty stage was only 2 % of the fuelled weight

parts.name: Steel balloon tank M (hydrolox)
parts.desc: Centaur-style: a paper-thin steel balloon of hydrogen over oxygen.
parts.role: The Centaur recipe: a pressure-stiffened steel balloon of hydrogen and oxygen, lighter than any other hydrogen tank.
parts.detail: Centaur, the upper stage that sent Surveyor, Voyager and Cassini on their way, is a steel balloon: walls half a millimetre thick, hydrogen on top, oxygen below, and between them a bulkhead of two steel skins on a fibreglass honeycomb that keeps the hydrogen from freezing the oxygen. It needs pressure every minute of its life, but it carries hydrogen for far less structure than any framed tank.
pros: Best Isp with a hydrolox engine
cons: Hydrogen boils off during the cruise
parts.real: Centaur III: 3.05 m wide, 12.7 m long, 20.8 t of propellant for 2.25 t dry, stainless walls 0.51 mm thick

parts.name: Intertank L
parts.desc: The unpressurised ring between two big tanks, where the loads come in.
parts.role: The stiff, unpressurised section between two large tanks: booster loads, equipment and umbilicals.
parts.detail: Between two tanks with separate domes sits a short hollow ring: the intertank. On the Shuttle's External Tank it carried the beam that took the push of both solid boosters, and the vents, valves and umbilical plates bolted to it without piercing a tank. Choose inside how it is built: skin and stringers, a machined grid, corrugated skin or carbon.
pros: Hard points without piercing a tank
cons: Mass and height that hold no propellant
parts.real: Shuttle External Tank intertank: 8.4 m wide, 6.9 m long, skin-stringer aluminium with ring frames and the SRB thrust beam

parts.name: Composite interstage L
parts.desc: Falcon 9's black interstage: carbon skins on an aluminium honeycomb.
parts.role: A light, stiff black ring of carbon fibre that tops the stage, with stowed grid fins and cold-gas thrusters.
parts.detail: The black band at the top of a Falcon 9 booster is its interstage: carbon-fibre skins bonded to an aluminium honeycomb core, far lighter than a metal ring of the same stiffness. It carries the four folded grid fins and the nitrogen thrusters the booster uses to turn around for landing. The construction is fixed: carbon sandwich.
pros: Places to hang thrusters and spheres
cons: Damage can hide under an intact skin
parts.real: Falcon 9 interstage: 4.5 m long, 3.7 m wide, carbon-fibre face sheets on an aluminium honeycomb core

parts.name: Instrument Unit
parts.desc: The Saturn V's brain: a wide ring of computers, gyros and radios.
parts.role: A wide guidance ring like the Saturn V's: flight computer, inertial platform, radios and cooling.
parts.detail: At the top of every Saturn V's third stage sat a ring less than a metre tall: the Instrument Unit. Around its inside wall IBM bolted the flight computer, the gyro-stabilised inertial platform, the radios, batteries and the water-cooled plates that kept them all at room temperature. It steered all three stages, from lift-off until the burn that sent Apollo towards the Moon. Reliability +3.5 %.
pros: Fits large stacks without an adapter
cons: Heaviest and most expensive guidance ring
parts.real: Saturn V Instrument Unit: 6.6 m wide, 0.91 m tall, about 2 t; LVDC computer and ST-124-M inertial platform, built by IBM

parts.name: External oxygen feed line
parts.desc: A big pipe down the outside of the tank, like the Shuttle tank's.
parts.role: Carries oxygen from the upper tank to the engines down the outside of the lower tank.
parts.detail: When oxygen sits above hydrogen, its pipe to the engines must get past the hydrogen tank. You can run it through the middle in an insulated tunnel, or outside along the wall, where it can be inspected and nothing freezes. The Shuttle's External Tank ran a pipe 43 cm wide (wider than a dinner plate) 21 m down its side, with two thin repressurisation lines beside it, bellows joints so it could flex, and brackets every few metres. Reliability +0.4 %.
cons: Ice can form on it on the pad
parts.real: Shuttle External Tank: a 43 cm (17 in) LOX feed line ran 21 m down the outside of the hydrogen tank, beside two 13 cm repressurisation lines

parts.name: Cable raceway, full length
parts.desc: A long, low fairing that carries every cable the length of the stage.
parts.role: A low aerodynamic channel running the full length of a long tank, full of cables and small lines.
parts.detail: Look at any Falcon 9 or Starship and you will see it: a narrow box running down the whole side of the stage. Inside it run the power and data cables from the top of the stage to the engines, the sensor wires, and small pressurisation lines. The ends slope like ramps so the airflow does not rip it off. Longer than a wiring tunnel, it protects more: reliability +1.2 %.
pros: Protects the cables of a whole long tank
parts.real: Falcon 9 and Starship external raceways; the Shuttle External Tank's cable trays behind their foam ramps

parts.name: COPV rack (3 helium bottles)
parts.desc: Three carbon-wrapped helium bottles on a rack: plenty of pressurant.
parts.role: Three composite-overwrapped pressure vessels of helium: enough gas to keep big tanks pressed full.
parts.detail: A COPV is a thin metal liner wound in carbon fibre: the lightest way to store gas at 300 to 400 bar. Big stages carry several, so one leaking bottle does not stop the flight. Three on a rack keep a large tank pressurised from lift-off to cut-off. Mind the stored energy: a COPV failure inside the oxygen tank destroyed a Falcon 9 and its satellite on the pad in 2016. Reliability +1 %.
pros: Plenty of pressurant, with a spare bottle
parts.real: Falcon 9 COPVs (inside the LOX tank; the AMOS-6 loss in 2016); Starship and Super Heavy COPV racks

parts.name: Intertank M
parts.desc: The ring between the oxygen tank above and the kerosene tank below, where boosters push.
parts.role: The stiff section between two medium tanks, oxygen above, fuel below: booster loads and equipment.
parts.detail: On the Soyuz core stage the four strap-on boosters push on the core through ball joints near the top of the stage, so the structure between the oxygen and kerosene tanks must carry the whole rocket's thrust into the core. Valves, cables and the nitrogen system bolt to it without piercing a tank. Choose inside how it is built.
pros: Hard points without piercing a tank
cons: Mass and height that hold no propellant
parts.real: Soyuz core stage (Blok A): 2.95 m wide; the boosters' thrust enters the core near its top, between the LOX and kerosene tanks

parts.name: Clustered tanks L (Saturn IB)
parts.desc: Nine tanks in a bundle: one wide oxygen tank in the middle, eight narrower tanks around it.
parts.role: A bundle of nine proven tanks instead of one big new one: 54 t of kerosene and liquid oxygen.
parts.detail: In 1958 nobody could build a 6.5 m tank quickly, so the Army rocket team at ABMA designed the first Saturn stage as a bundle of tanks it already knew how to make (the Saturn I first flew in 1961): a Jupiter-sized oxygen tank in the middle and eight Redstone-sized tanks around it, four of oxygen and four of kerosene in turn, tied together at the top by a spider beam. Every tank is small, so it is easy to build, test and carry. The price is nine sets of walls and domes, and the gaps between the tanks hold nothing.
pros: Proven tanks: cheap to build and carry
cons: Heavy: nine sets of walls and domes
The gaps between the tanks hold no propellant
parts.real: Saturn IB first stage S-IB (Chrysler, 1966–75): 6.53 m wide, 24.5 m long; one 2.67 m LOX tank and eight 1.78 m tanks (4 LOX, 4 RP-1); about 400 t of propellant for about 42 t dry with 8 H-1 engines

parts.name: Clustered storable tanks L (Proton)
parts.desc: A wide oxidizer tank in the middle, six fuel tanks around it, each with its own engine below.
parts.role: Proton's first stage: a central oxidizer tank ringed by six fuel tanks, every piece narrow enough for a railway wagon.
parts.detail: The 4.1 m central tank was the widest load the railways could carry, so the rest went into six 1.6 m tanks around it, and each outer tank carries one engine at its foot. The real stage burns nitrogen tetroxide and UDMH, which ignite on contact and stay liquid for months. This game has no storable propellant, so here it burns as kerolox, the nearest in density and Isp.
pros: Every piece fits on a train
cons: The gaps between the tanks hold no propellant
parts.real: Proton first stage (1965–): central N2O4 tank 4.1 m wide, six UDMH tanks 1.6 m, 7.4 m across, 21 m long; about 420 t of propellant for 30.6 t dry (Proton-M) with six RD-275 engines; the width was set by the rail loading gauge

parts.name: Spherical tanks in a cone (N1)
parts.desc: Two ball-shaped tanks, kerosene above oxygen, inside a shell that narrows towards the top.
parts.role: The N1 first stage: two spheres, the strongest tank shape there is, hung inside a tapering shell.
parts.detail: A sphere holds the most for the least wall, and the N1 spheres could be welded at the launch site from pieces that came by train. But round tanks leave the corners of a cone empty: the N1 first stage was 17 m wide at the base, and much of that width held only air. The conical shell around the spheres carried the loads. All four N1 launches failed, from engine, control and feed-line problems, not from the tanks themselves.
pros: Spheres: the lightest wall for what they hold
Built from pieces that travel by rail
cons: Wastes the space in the cone: only 18 t
parts.real: N1 Block A (1969–72): 30.1 m long, a cone from 16.9 m at the base to 10.3 m at the top; a smaller kerosene sphere above a larger LOX sphere, hung in the load-bearing shell; about 1,880 t at lift-off with 30 NK-15 engines

parts.name: Soyuz core tanks (Blok A)
parts.desc: The R-7's waisted core: an oxygen tank of two cones over a narrower kerosene tank.
parts.role: The most-flown rocket body: the Soyuz core stage, widest at the ring where the four boosters push.
parts.detail: The Soyuz core is not a straight tube. Its oxygen tank is two cones joined at a stiff ring, and that ring is where the noses of the four strap-on boosters push the whole rocket. Below it the core narrows, so the boosters can hug it. Boiled liquid nitrogen pressurises the tanks. The design comes from the 1957 R-7 missile and still flies.
cons: Narrow waist: less room for side equipment
parts.real: Soyuz core stage Block A: 2.95 m at its widest, 27.1 m long; 63.8 t LOX and 26.3 t kerosene for about 6.5 t dry; tanks pressurised by evaporated liquid nitrogen (Arianespace Soyuz user's manual, 2012)

parts.name: Soyuz third-stage tanks (Blok I)
parts.desc: Kerosene on top, then the instrument section, then oxygen: the Soyuz upper stage.
parts.role: A short medium tank pair with the instrument section between the kerosene above and the oxygen below.
parts.detail: Unusually, the Soyuz third stage carries its fuel on top. Between the kerosene and the oxygen sits a short ring with hatches, full of control equipment. The stage stands on an open lattice so its engine can light while the core below is still firing. The instrument ring counts as guidance equipment: reliability +1 %, not added on top of another guidance ring.
parts.real: Soyuz Block I (1960–): 2.66 m wide, 6.7 m long; 25.4 t of LOX and kerosene for 2.36 t dry (Soyuz-2.1b, RD-0124); kerosene tank, instrument section, LOX tank, top to bottom

parts.name: Storable-propellant tanks M (Titan II)
parts.desc: Gemini's launcher: oxidizer over fuel in two stiff aluminium tanks.
parts.role: Titan II's first stage: two separate tanks stiff enough to stand empty, the oxidizer pipe running down through the fuel.
parts.detail: Titan II was a missile that waited fuelled in a silo for years, so it used propellants that stay liquid at room temperature: nitrogen tetroxide and Aerozine 50, which ignite the moment they touch. The oxidizer pipe runs down through the fuel tank inside a conduit; the tube on the outside carries the wiring. For the Gemini astronauts, standpipes and an accumulator were added to stop the pogo shaking. This game has no storable propellant, so here it burns as kerolox, the nearest in density and Isp.
parts.real: Titan II GLV first stage (1964–66): 3.05 m wide, about 21 m long; N2O4 tank above an Aerozine 50 tank; about 117 t of propellant for 4.3 to 6.7 t dry (sources differ); the 10 in oxidizer line runs through the fuel tank

parts.name: Storable common-bulkhead tank M (PSLV)
parts.desc: India's PSLV second stage: two propellants, one shared bulkhead and a ring of water at the bottom.
parts.role: The PSLV second stage: a common-bulkhead tank of storable propellant, with a ring-shaped water tank for the engine.
parts.detail: The Vikas engine sprays water into the hot gas that drives its turbine, so the stage carries a ring-shaped (toroidal) water tank at its base. The two propellants, UH25 (mostly UDMH) and nitrogen tetroxide, share one bulkhead, and helium pressurises them and the water. This game has no storable propellant, so here it burns as kerolox, the nearest in density and Isp.
pros: One bulkhead: short for what it holds
cons: The water tank is mass that does not burn
parts.real: PSLV second stage PS2 (ISRO, 1993–): 2.8 m wide, 12.8 m long, 41.5 t of UH25 and N2O4 in two tanks separated by a common bulkhead, toroidal water tank at the bottom, helium pressurisation; Vikas engine, 799 kN

parts.name: Common-bulkhead hydrolox tank L (Ariane 5)
parts.desc: Ariane 5's core: oxygen on top of hydrogen, one bulkhead between them.
parts.role: Europe's main stage: one long aluminium tank, liquid oxygen above liquid hydrogen, split by a single bulkhead.
parts.detail: Ariane 5's core stage is one 5.4 m tank divided by a common bulkhead: the heavy oxygen on top, the bulky hydrogen below. When the stage was upgraded, the bulkhead was moved down to fit 16 t more oxygen. A thin foam layer outside keeps the cold in. Helium pushes the oxygen; hydrogen gas bled from the engine pushes the hydrogen.
pros: 28 t of hydrogen and oxygen in one tank
Best Isp with a hydrolox engine
cons: A bulkhead leak mixes the propellants: reliability 99.6 %
parts.real: Ariane 5 EPC (1996–2023): 5.4 m wide, 23.8 m long without the engine; ECA version 150 t LOX and 25 t LH2 for 14.7 t dry; common bulkhead; LOX pressurised by helium, LH2 by hydrogen gas from the Vulcain 2

parts.name: Upper-stage hydrogen tank L (Delta IV, SLS ICPS)
parts.desc: A wide, short tank of liquid hydrogen, built to hang the oxygen tank below it.
parts.role: The hydrogen half of a cryogenic upper stage: a wide tank on top, with a smaller oxygen tank hung under it.
parts.detail: Hydrogen takes up most of the volume, so on the Delta Cryogenic Second Stage it gets the full 5 m width, and the much denser oxygen sits below in a small round tank hung from a truss. The same stage pushed Orion towards the Moon on Artemis I and II as the SLS Interim Cryogenic Propulsion Stage. Sprayed and bonded foam and helium-purged blankets keep the hydrogen liquid; the outside is finished white.
pros: Best Isp with a hydrolox engine
cons: Little propellant mass for its size
parts.real: Delta Cryogenic Second Stage (Delta III and IV, 1998–2024; 5 m version on Delta IV) and SLS ICPS (Artemis I 2022, Artemis II 2026): 5.1 m wide, 13.7 m long with the engine; 27.2 t of propellant for 3.49 t empty; isogrid aluminium, spun-formed domes, spray-on and bond-on insulation with helium-purged blankets

parts.name: Hung oxygen tank (Delta IV upper stage)
parts.desc: A small, round oxygen tank hung under the hydrogen tank, inside the skirt.
parts.role: The oxygen half of a cryogenic upper stage: a squat, round tank hung on a truss below the hydrogen.
parts.detail: Liquid oxygen is sixteen times denser than liquid hydrogen, so the same mass fits in a much smaller tank. On the 4 m Delta IV upper stage it is a 3.2 m squashed ball (an oblate spheroid); the 5 m stage lengthens it. It hangs below the hydrogen tank on a composite truss, with the avionics shelf on its lower dome. During the climb it rides inside the interstage, so here the skin covers it. On the real stage this small tank holds most of the propellant mass; here each tank holds the mix by volume.
pros: Compact: dense oxygen in a small tank
A shelf for avionics on its dome
cons: Rides inside a skirt: extra skin mass
parts.real: Delta IV DCSS: a 3.2 m LO2 tank (an oblate spheroid on the 4 m stage, lengthened on the 5 m stage) hung from a composite intertank truss; avionics on an equipment shelf on its aft dome (ULA Delta IV documents)

look.shape: lengthened oblate tank 0.63 R on a black composite truss, silver blanket

parts.name: Orthogrid methalox tank L (Vulcan)
parts.desc: Vulcan's booster: oxygen over liquefied natural gas, one common bulkhead, orthogrid aluminium.
parts.role: A big aluminium tank of methane and oxygen, its walls machined into a square grid, the two split by one bulkhead.
parts.detail: United Launch Alliance builds Vulcan's 5.4 m booster from aluminium barrels machined into an orthogrid (square pockets) and spun-formed domes, with liquid oxygen on top, liquefied natural gas (mostly methane) below and a common bulkhead between them. The oxygen reaches the two BE-4 engines through a big pipe down the outside of the fuel tank.
parts.real: Vulcan first stage (2024–): 5.4 m wide, 33.3 m long; about 353 t of LO2 and LNG for 28.6 t dry; orthogrid aluminium barrels, spun-formed domes, common bulkhead, external LO2 feed line (ULA)

parts.name: Centerbody section L
parts.desc: The stiff ring between a large oxygen tank above and a hydrogen tank below.
parts.role: The structure between two large separate tanks, where equipment, umbilicals and the pad swing arms connect.
parts.detail: On the Delta IV core the oxygen tank sits above the hydrogen tank, and between them is a short unpressurised ring: the centerbody, a composite shell. It carries the loads from one tank to the other, and the pad swing arms plug into it. Choose inside how it is built.
pros: Hard points without piercing a tank
cons: Mass and height that hold no propellant
parts.real: Delta IV common booster core: composite centerbody between the LO2 and LH2 tanks, where the swing arms connect (ULA Delta IV user's guide)

parts.name: Forward skirt L
parts.desc: The ring on top of a large stage: vents, instruments and the joint to the next section.
parts.role: A short, stiff ring above the top tank: a dry bay for instruments and vents, and the joint to whatever sits above.
parts.detail: Big stages start with a forward skirt. On Saturn V's first stage it was corrugated aluminium and held the telemetry, the range-safety receivers and the oxygen vents; on the S-II it was a thin skin with hat-shaped stringers outside. Equipment rides inside it, out of the airflow, without a single hole in a tank.
pros: Stiff joint to the section above
parts.real: Saturn V S-IC forward skirt (corrugated 7075 aluminium, telemetry and LOX vents); S-II forward skirt (7075 skin 1 mm thick with external hat-section stringers); Atlas V forward adapter skirt (2014 aluminium isogrid)

parts.name: Aft skirt L
parts.desc: The ring below the bottom tank: attitude thrusters, ullage motors and helium bottles bolt to it.
parts.role: A short ring under the lowest tank that carries side hardware: thruster pods, ullage motors, helium bottles.
parts.detail: The Saturn S-IVB's aft skirt carried its two auxiliary propulsion modules, which held the stage steady in orbit, and two small solid motors that settled the propellant before the engine lit. Mounting them on a dry skirt keeps them off the tank walls.
pros: Hard points for thrusters and bottles
parts.real: Saturn S-IVB aft skirt: two APS modules 180° apart and two TX-280 ullage motors; S-II aft skirt (7075 skin 1.8 mm with external stringers)

parts.name: Forward skirt with flight computers (SLS)
parts.desc: The SLS core stage forward skirt: three flight computers and the stage avionics.
parts.role: A large forward skirt that houses the flight computers and guidance electronics of the whole vehicle.
parts.detail: On the Space Launch System the three flight computers and much of the core stage avionics ride in the forward skirt, the ring above the oxygen tank. They vote on every decision, so one can fail and the flight goes on. A dedicated guidance section catches faults the capsule computer would miss: reliability +3 %.
pros: Room for the whole avionics suite
parts.real: SLS core stage forward skirt, 8.4 m wide: the three flight computers and avionics, with more boxes in the intertank and engine section (NASA, Boeing)

parts.name: Hot-staging lattice M (Soyuz, N1)
parts.desc: An open lattice of struts: the engine above can fire through it.
parts.role: An open truss between two sections: light, and open so an engine's exhaust can escape through it.
parts.detail: Soyuz lights its third stage while the core below is still burning: the flame escapes through the open lattice that joins them, and a shield protects the top of the core. Hot staging needs no small motors to settle the propellant. This ship flies as one stage, so here the lattice is simply light, open structure.
pros: Open: the equipment inside is easy to reach
cons: No skin to shelter equipment from the airflow
A heat shield on the dome below adds mass
parts.real: Soyuz: the truss between Block A and Block I lets the third stage ignite before separation (Arianespace Soyuz user's manual, 2012); 2.66 m. N1: Warren-truss open-strut interstages above Block A

parts.name: Hot-staging lattice L (Proton)
parts.desc: A wide open lattice of struts that an engine can fire through.
parts.role: A large open truss between two big sections: light, and open for the exhaust of an engine that lights inside it.
parts.detail: Proton's second stage starts its engines a moment before it lets go of the first stage; the exhaust blows out through the gaps of an aluminium lattice. This ship flies as one stage, so here the lattice is simply light, open structure.
pros: Open: the equipment inside is easy to reach
cons: No skin to shelter equipment from the airflow
A heat shield on the dome below adds mass
parts.real: Proton: a lattice of V95 aluminium alloy between the first and second stages lets the second-stage exhaust escape at about T+120 s (RussianSpaceWeb)

parts.name: Vented hot-staging ring L (Super Heavy)
parts.desc: A short steel ring full of vents on top of the booster: the ship lights its engines through it.
parts.role: Starship's hot-staging ring: a steel band with big vents, so the ship's engines can fire while it still sits on the booster.
parts.detail: From Flight 2 in November 2023, Starship separates by lighting its engines while still attached. The flame escapes through the vents of a ring on top of Super Heavy, and a shield protects the booster's dome. On Block 3 boosters the ring is built into the top of the methane tank. Welded stainless steel, like the rest of the booster: the material is fixed.
pros: Stiff joint to the section above
parts.real: Super Heavy vented interstage (Flight 2, 18 Nov 2023, onward): about 2 m tall on the 9 m booster, which is 71 m with it and 69 m without; integrated into the forward dome on Block 3

parts.name: Auxiliary propulsion module (S-IVB)
parts.desc: A pod of small thrusters on the side of the stage: holds the attitude and settles the propellant.
parts.role: A self-contained pod of small thrusters that steers the stage in orbit and gives a gentle push before the main engine restarts.
parts.detail: The Saturn S-IVB carried two of these pods on its aft skirt, 180° apart. Each held three 667 N attitude thrusters and one 311 N ullage engine, with their own small tanks of storable propellant. The ullage push settles the propellant over the outlets so the main engine restarts on liquid, not gas. Reliability +0.4 %, shared with the ullage motors.
pros: Settles the propellant before a restart
parts.real: Saturn S-IVB APS: two modules, each with three 150 lbf (667 N) TR-204 thrusters and one 70 lbf (311 N) ullage engine, about 52 kg MMH and 68 kg N2O4

parts.name: Solid ullage motor
parts.desc: A small solid rocket that gives the stage a short push before the engine lights.
parts.role: A small solid rocket fired for a few seconds before ignition, so the propellant settles over the tank outlets.
parts.detail: In weightlessness, or the moment the stage below stops pushing, the propellant floats away from the outlets and the engine would gulp gas. A few seconds of push from a small solid motor settles it. The S-II carried four on its interstage, the S-IVB two on its aft skirt. Reliability +0.4 %, shared with the auxiliary propulsion module.
parts.real: Saturn S-IVB: two Thiokol TX-280 motors, 3,420 lbf (15.2 kN) for 3.8 s each; S-II: four of eight possible ullage motors, 22,700 lbf (101 kN) for 3.7 s
